content: 1. A study conducted by Ell J, Sagno JB, et al., published in PLOS ONE in 2013, evaluated the outcomes of maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV in Malawi. The research assessed both maternal and infant health outcomes two years post-delivery. 2. O’Brien L, Shaffer N, Sangrujee N, and Abimbola TO analyzed the incremental costs associated with transitioning from Option B to Option B+ for PMTCT of HIV. Their findings, published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2014, highlighted the financial implications of this policy shift. 3. Fasawé O, Avila C, Shaffer N, Schouten E, Chimbwandira F, Hoos D, and colleagues conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of Option B+ for HIV prevention and treatment in mothers and children in Malawi. Their results were published in PLOS ONE in 2013. 4. Van Deusen A, Paintsil E, Agyarko-Poku T, and Long EF examined the cost-effectiveness of Option B+ for PMTCT of HIV in resource-limited settings, using evidence from Kumasi, Ghana. Their findings were published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2015. 5. Ciaranello AL, Perez F, Engelsman B, Walensky RP, Mushavi A, et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of the 2010 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for PMTCT of HIV in Zimbabwe. Their study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2013, provided insights into the economic and health impacts of these guidelines. 6. Gopalappa C, Stover J, Shaffer N, and Mahy M analyzed the costs and benefits of Option B+ for PMTCT of HIV. Their findings, published in AIDS in 2014, emphasized the economic and health advantages of this approach. 7. Ishikawa N, Shimbo T, Miyano S, Sikazwe I, Mwango A, et al. assessed the health outcomes and cost impact of the 2013 WHO guidelines on PMTCT of HIV in Zambia. Their study was published in PLOS ONE in 2014. 8. Adesina A and Alkenbrack S summarized the costs and impacts of scaling up PMTCT services in Nigeria, based on findings from 13 Nigerian states. This report was part of the Health Policy Project in 2015, supported by USAID and PEPFAR. 9. Erekaha S, et al. conducted a qualitative study on the readiness of women living with HIV in rural Nigeria to adopt Option B+. This unpublished study was presented as a poster at the 10th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne, Australia, in 2014. 10. Ngariña M, Tarimo EA, Naburi H, Kilewo C, Mwanyika-Sando M, et al. explored women’s preferences regarding infant or maternal antiretroviral prophylaxis for PMTCT of HIV during breastfeeding and their views on Option B+ in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Their findings were published in PLOS ONE in 2014. 11. Hsieh AC, Mburu G, Garner AB, Teltschik A, Ram M, et al. gathered community and service provider perspectives to inform the 2013 WHO consolidated antiretroviral guidelines. Their key findings and lessons learned were published in AIDS in 2014. 12. The Salamander Trust conducted a global survey to identify key values and preferences regarding the sexual and reproductive health and human rights of women living with HIV. The findings were published by the WHO in 2014. 13. Price AJ, et al. conducted a retrospective cohort study on the uptake of PMTCT using Option B+ in northern rural Malawi. Their study, published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2014, highlighted the program's effectiveness. 14. The 2013 WHO antiretroviral guidelines recommended initiating ART in all children with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) regardless of age or CD4 count. Additionally, ART initiation was advised for all children under five years of age, irrespective of CD4 count or clinical stage. 15. Infants diagnosed as HIV-positive within the first year of life were strongly recommended to start ART, supported by moderate-quality evidence. For children aged 12 to 59 months, the recommendation was conditional, based on very low-quality evidence. 16. The guidelines emphasized the need to prioritize children under two years of age due to their higher mortality risk. Simplifying eligibility criteria for ART initiation was suggested to improve health outcomes for children living with HIV, especially in settings with limited access to immunological testing. 17. Despite the global recommendation to treat all children under five years of age, some countries, such as Cameroon and Kenya, adopted policies to treat children under ten years due to concerns about poor adherence among adolescents. 18. Poor adherence, unreliable drug supply for children, and challenges in providing care by healthcare workers remain significant barriers to implementing these recommendations effectively. 19. The Clinical Guideline Development Group was tasked with re-examining available evidence and considering the risks and benefits of treating all children under 15 years of age, regardless of clinical and immunological criteria. 20. Sub-Saharan African countries, including Ethiopia, Namibia, South Sudan, Uganda, and Tanzania, have broadly adopted the recommendation to treat all children and adolescents under 15 years of age, irrespective of clinical and immunological conditions. 21. Limited access to CD4 testing and poor clinical staging practices continue to hinder treatment initiation for eligible children and adolescents in many settings. 22. Evidence from randomized controlled trials and causal modeling analyses suggests that earlier ART initiation results in lower mortality and better growth outcomes for children and adolescents living with HIV.
